newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish voters give verdict on constitution dispute.
newsitem.headline: Polish voters give verdict on constitution dispute.

text.p: Polish voters faced a choice in a referendum on Sunday between adopting a new constitution sponsored by the ruling ex-communists or heeding fervent calls from the rightist opposition to reject it.
The charter is meant to enshrine liberties gained with the fall of communism in 1989 and stabilise Poland's democracy.
But the Solidarity trade union and allied parties say it fails to reflect Poland's Roman Catholic, patriotic heritage, to guarantee sovereignty or settle communist-era wrongs.

The Solidarity Election Action (AWS) alliance, under-represented in parliament but rivalling the ex-communists for top place in opinion polls before elections due in September, is angry it is being pushed through now.
Union leader Marian Krzaklewski said that for this parliament to adopt what he termed an atheistic constitution before the elections would "place a time bomb under Poland".

The constitution was co-authored by two parliamentary opposition parties descended from the pre-1989 fight for democracy, in a compromise with the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and its Peasant allies in government.
Its supporters say it embraces all, believers or not.

"We, the Polish Nation, all Citizens of the Republic, equally those believing in God as the source of truth, justice, goodness and beauty and those not sharing that faith and drawing these universal values from other sources..." it reads.

"This is a good constitution, worthy of our past, allowing us to do justice to our national aspirations," President Aleksander Kwasniewski, a former communist turned social democrat, said in televised address on late on Friday.
Above all, he urged Poles to take part in the referendum.
Opinion polls suggested the constitution was likely to pass but that many Poles, baffled by the 243-article document and conflicting accounts of what it means, would not vote.
The vote will be legally binding no matter how few take part but a low turnout would keep the debate raging.
A "no" verdict would leave Poland with remains of its discredited 1952 constitution, amended by 1992 interim laws, until some future parliament can agree on a new version.

The unwieldy new constitution broadly retains the current political system while weakening the presidency. It sets caps on the government's spending but obliges it to support employment and home building.

Solidarity, seeing Poland's history as bound up with the majority Catholic faith, wanted the charter to clearly invoke God, place religious values above man-made law and include a clause effectively banning abortion -- now legal in Poland.
The bishops, greatly concerned over abortion, have announced deep moral reservations about the current document.
The right also says a section permitting Poland to surrender by treaty some functions to international organisations -- to ease entry into European structures -- limits sovereignty.
The constitution's authors reject these arguments as false.
In the end, many voting against the charter did so from disgust that the ex-communists, late converts and beneficiaries of democracy, were assuming the honour of crowning it.
"The SLD, its constitution, and all that those people stand for just rub me up the wrong way," said Krystyna Luty, a 55-year-old lawyer voting at a busy Warsaw polling station.
The voting may give clues to broad party sympathies ahead of the election, and indicate attitudes towards the Church just before a May 31-June 10 visit by Polish Pope John Paul ll.
Solidarity spokesman Piotr Zak said this month his grouping would not be devastated if the constitution passed and would see it as a defeat only if the voting was three to one.
Various other commentators said the referendum would not necessarily be a dry-run for the general elections.
But the ex-communist's party leader Jozef Oleksy, scenting victory as he cast his vote, told reporters the outcome could prefigure the verdict of the parliamentary elections.
Polling stations were due to close at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) -- with exit poll results to be announced minutes later and the official verdict due by Tuesday.
